lines.say: Our review pipeline has one reviewer for everything: SQL, threads, tests. One prompt can't be an expert in all of them.
Today, you'll add routing: a small, fast model reads the file, and sends it to the right specialist.
And Java's compiler will make sure no case is forgotten.

lines.say: So, what is routing?
A router agent looks at the input, and puts it in a category.
Each category has its own specialist agent.
Specialists get focused prompts, so each one is better at its job than a generalist.
And only one specialist runs: the one that fits. You don't pay for the others.

lines.say: When should you route?
When inputs fall into clear categories, each category needs a different prompt or tools, and classifying is easy.
Don't route when one prompt already handles everything, or when categories overlap. And if an input needs several specialists at once, that's parallel agents: the next episode.

lines.say: Here's our use case.
In episode two, one generalist reviewer handled every file, with one prompt, on the big model.
Now a Haiku router reads the file first, and picks one of four specialists: security, concurrency, testing, or code quality.
Here's the reviewer from episode two.

    <dependencies>
        <!-- The official Anthropic Java SDK -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.anthropic</groupId>
            <artifactId>anthropic-java</artifactId>
            <version>3.3.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- Lets us run the router with: mvn compile exec:java -->

        </plugins>

</project>

    static final Agent ROUTER = new Agent("Router",
            "claude-haiku-5-5",

lines.say: One: the model is Haiku 5.5. Small and fast.
lines.tts: One: the model is Haiku five point five. Small and fast.

lines.say: Two: the prompt defines each category in a few words. Clear categories make reliable routing.
And three: no tools. The router only classifies. It never fixes anything.
Step four: route to the specialists. First, a switch from each specialist to its focus.
This is a switch expression on an enum, with no default. So it must cover every value.
If I add a fifth specialist to the enum and forget it here, the code doesn't even compile.

lines.say: Then the specialists. Each one is the same Agent class, with a focused prompt and the read file tool.
Now main. The router gets the code directly in its task. That's one cheap call, with no tool loop.
I print the route and its reason. Then the chosen specialist does the real review, on the big model.

lines.say: Four tips for your router.
One: use a small model, and define each category in a few clear words.
Two: return an enum, and switch on it with no default. The compiler checks every route for you.
Three: always have a fallback category, like GENERAL, for inputs that fit nowhere.
And four: log the router's reason. When a file goes to the wrong expert, you'll see why.

scenes.heading: Recap
items: A **small model** decides, a strong model works
An [[enum + switch]] makes every route compile-checked

lines.say: Let's recap.
Routing means a router classifies the input, and only the right specialist runs.
A small, cheap model makes the decision. A strong model does the work.
And in Java, an enum with an exhaustive switch makes every route checked by the compiler.
